rules.statement: Don't report an `IValidateOptions<T>` implementation for taking a framework singleton such as `IHostEnvironment` in its constructor; the rule only forbids options validation that constructs strategies with their own dependency graphs.
rules.why: The rule exists because resolving a dependency graph inside `IOptions<T>.Value` can deadlock composition, and a framework singleton with no dependencies and no options read can't cause that.
rules.check: Before flagging a validator's constructor dependency, see whether it is a framework singleton with no dependency graph and no options read, or a service whose resolution builds further dependencies or reads options.

rules.statement: Don't ask a composition-root package to move its public registration marker type into an Abstractions package; a composition root declares its marker next to its builder.
rules.why: Any package that composes the feature references the composition root anyway, so an Abstractions package would hold nothing but the marker.
rules.check: Before flagging a public marker declared in an implementation package, check whether the package is documented (for example in an ADR) as a composition root.

rules.statement: In a test project, don't flag `null!` used to pass a deliberate null to the code under test, as in an argument-validation test; the test conventions allow that one use.
rules.why: These tests have to pass a null on purpose to prove the code rejects it, and the test conventions name this as the allowed use of the null-forgiving operator.
rules.check: Look at whether the `!` value goes straight to the code under test to exercise null handling; flag only other uses.

rules.statement: Before reporting that code or a test contradicts an ADR, check whether a later ADR amends that decision.
rules.why: A later decision can amend an earlier one, with the amendment named in the earlier ADR's Status, so the code and the decision record may already agree.
rules.check: Read the cited ADR's Status and search the other ADRs for amendments to the decision before flagging the disagreement.

rules.statement: Cap any computed `setTimeout` delay well below 2^31-1 ms, for example at the regular poll interval, so a far-off deadline never arms a timer that fires at once.
rules.why: Browsers treat a delay above 2^31-1 ms (about 24.8 days) as 0. A timer that re-arms itself then runs in a tight loop.
rules.check: Look for `setTimeout` calls whose delay comes from a remote timestamp or lifetime and has no upper bound.

rules.statement: Don't silently skip a configuration entry that is only partly configured: log a warning (or fail) that names the missing keys, and treat only an entry that sets nothing as inert.
rules.why: A silent skip leaves the developer with an unexplained failure somewhere else instead of a message that names the missing setting.
rules.check: Look for code that skips a configured entry when some required values are missing, and check whether it reports which keys are missing.

rules.statement: A seeder that owns a record must reconcile an existing record with the current configuration, replacing it and logging the replacement when they differ, instead of returning early because a record with that id exists.
rules.why: With add-only seeding, changed keys or URIs never reach the stored record, and the resulting failures don't point to the seeder.
rules.check: Look for seed code that returns as soon as an entity with the same id exists, without comparing its stored settings to the configured ones.

rules.statement: When two constants name the same location or value, derive one from the other instead of defining both independently.
rules.why: If one is renamed without the other, the mismatch fails silently at runtime (for example, every asset returns 404) instead of at startup.
rules.check: Look for literal constants in different types that encode the same path, name or value.

rules.statement: Don't null-check a non-nullable property that always has a default instance; either drop the check or make the property's nullability match it.
rules.why: The check hides the contract that the value is always present.
rules.check: Look for `is not null` or `!= null` checks on members declared non-nullable with a default initializer.

rules.statement: Remove a DOM element created only to perform one action, such as a hidden form used to submit a POST, right after the action.
rules.why: Repeated calls, in tests or when the browser doesn't navigate away, otherwise leave stray nodes in the DOM.
rules.check: Look for elements appended to `document.body` for a one-off action and never removed.

rules.statement: In an ASP.NET Core host, fail startup in Production when `AllowedHosts` is missing, empty or contains `*`, and don't set `AllowedHosts` to `*` in the base `appsettings.json`.
rules.why: With host filtering off, forged `Host` headers reach code that builds callback and logout URIs.
rules.check: Look for `AllowedHosts: "*"` in base settings, and for a host that has no production check of host filtering.

rules.statement: When a validation or error message includes a configured URL, show it without user info, query or fragment.
rules.why: Those URL parts can carry secrets, and the message ends up in logs and startup errors.
rules.check: Look for failure messages that interpolate a raw configured URL value.
